subject: Copywriting
title: Tone and Voice in Email
description: A 60-second lesson on Tone and Voice in Email.

hook.text: Mailchimp's voice guide says: 'Write like a smart friend who explains things well.' That tone built a $12B brand.

buildup.text: Email is the most intimate marketing channel. It arrives in a personal inbox alongside family and friend messages.

discovery.text: Emails written in a conversational, first-person tone get 25% more replies than formal, corporate-sounding ones.

twist.text: Too casual backfires in finance, healthcare, and law. A bank that writes like a teenager loses credibility instantly.

climax.text: The best email voices match the audience's expectations.

punchline.text: Write like a smart friend. Match your audience's expectations.

quiz.question: How much more do conversational emails get replied to?

details.summary: Email tone sits between formal business writing and casual conversation. The best email copy uses a consistent brand voice while adapting tone to context — welcome emails feel warm, abandoned cart emails feel urgent, and re-engagement emails feel personal. Voice stays constant; tone flexes.
details.whyItMatters: Inconsistent tone confuses subscribers and erodes brand trust. Understanding the voice-versus-tone distinction helps writers maintain brand coherence while adapting to different email scenarios.
takeaways: Voice is your brand personality — it stays consistent across all emails
Tone adapts to the situation while remaining true to the brand voice
Write emails as if speaking to one person, not broadcasting to a list

faq.question: What is the difference between voice and tone in email?
faq.answer: Voice is who you are — it never changes. Mailchimp's voice is always witty and informal. Tone is how you adapt to situations — a sale announcement is exciting, a security alert is serious. Same voice, different tones for different contexts.

faq.question: How do you find the right tone for marketing emails?
faq.answer: Start with how you'd speak to the subscriber in person. Then adjust for context: warm for welcome emails, direct for promotions, empathetic for re-engagement. Read every email aloud before sending — if it sounds robotic or forced, the tone needs adjustment.
